claim: Kinetochores contain multiple copies of the microtubule-binding NDC80 complex as an evolutionary conserved feature.
source: Presence of multiple copies of the microtubule-binding NDC80 complex is an evolutionary conserved feature of kinetochores, points of attachment of chromosomes to spindle microtubules.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known feature of kinetochores.

claim: Single NDC80 complexes do not track depolymerizing microtubules.
source: while single NDC80 complexes do not track depolymerizing microtubules, reconstituted particles containing the NDC80 receptor CENP-T bound to three or more NDC80 complexes do so effectively
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Reconstituted particles containing CENP-T bound to three or more NDC80 complexes effectively track depolymerizing microtubules.
source: while single NDC80 complexes do not track depolymerizing microtubules, reconstituted particles containing the NDC80 receptor CENP-T bound to three or more NDC80 complexes do so effectively, as expected for a kinetochore force coupler.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 1.

claim: The residence time of modules on microtubules increases exponentially with the number of NDC80 complexes.
source: The modules' residence time on microtubules increased exponentially with the number of NDC80 complexes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 2E.

claim: Modules with two or more NDC80 complexes track depolymerizing microtubules with increasing efficiencies.
source: Modules with two or more complexes tracked depolymerizing microtubules with increasing efficiencies
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: Modules with two or more NDC80 complexes stalled microtubule depolymerization in a force-dependent manner when conjugated to cargo.
source: Modules with two or more complexes tracked depolymerizing microtubules with increasing efficiencies, and stalled and rescued microtubule depolymerization in a force-dependent manner when conjugated to cargo.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: Modules with two or more NDC80 complexes rescued microtubule depolymerization in a force-dependent manner when conjugated to cargo.
source: Modules with two or more complexes tracked depolymerizing microtubules with increasing efficiencies, and stalled and rescued microtubule depolymerization in a force-dependent manner when conjugated to cargo.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: NDC80 tracks depolymerizing microtubules by harnessing force generated during microtubule disassembly rather than through biased diffusion.
source: Our observations indicate that NDC80, rather than through biased diffusion, tracks depolymerizing microtubules by harnessing force generated during microtubule disassembly.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, based on the experimental observations.

claim: Multivalent ligands may have increased binding affinity for multimeric targets compared to equivalent monovalent ligands.
source: While it is well established that multivalent ligands may have increased binding affinity for multimeric targets in comparison to equivalent monovalent ligands, the quantitative effects of multivalency for macromolecular interactions cannot be easily predicted (Jencks, 1981), and needs therefore to be determined experimentally.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation to Jencks, 1981.

claim: The quantitative effects of multivalency for macromolecular interactions cannot be easily predicted and need to be determined experimentally.
source: While it is well established that multivalent ligands may have increased binding affinity for multimeric targets in comparison to equivalent monovalent ligands, the quantitative effects of multivalency for macromolecular interactions cannot be easily predicted (Jencks, 1981), and needs therefore to be determined experimentally.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Jencks, 1981.

claim: Kinetochores are multiprotein assemblies built on the centromeres of chromosomes.
source: Kinetochores are multiprotein assemblies built on the centromeres of chromosomes (Musacchio and Desai, 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: The ability of kinetochores to hold on to the ends of microtubules is crucial for the segregation of replicated chromosomes during cell division.
source: Their ability to hold on to the ends of microtubules, dynamic polymers that alternate between phases of growth and shrinkage, is crucial for the segregation of replicated chromosomes (sister chromatids) to the daughter cells during cell division.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about kinetochore function.

claim: Chromosome propulsion during cell division does not require molecular motors.
source: This event does not require molecular motors, and chromosome propulsion is mediated by the ability of kinetochores to remain attached to depolymerizing microtubules (Grishchuk and McIntosh, 2006; Tanaka et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: Chromosome propulsion is mediated by the ability of kinetochores to remain attached to depolymerizing microtubules.
source: This event does not require molecular motors, and chromosome propulsion is mediated by the ability of kinetochores to remain attached to depolymerizing microtubules (Grishchuk and McIntosh, 2006; Tanaka et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: A single NDC80 complex is unable to follow dynamic microtubules in vitro.
source: In vitro reconstitution reveals that a single NDC80 complex is unable to follow dynamic microtubules (Powers et al., 2009; Schmidt et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous studies.

claim: Microtubule end-tracking activity is conferred to NDC80 by the presence of Dam1 or Ska complexes.
source: Microtubule end-tracking activity is conferred to NDC80 by the presence of Dam1 or Ska complexes, which provide additional binding sites to microtubule walls and dynamic ends (Tien et al., 2010; Lampert et al., 2010; Schmidt et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous studies.

claim: NDC80 gains tip-tracking properties in the presence of factors that trigger multimerization, such as functionalized bead surfaces or antibodies.
source: NDC80 was also shown to gain tip-tracking properties in the presence of factors that trigger multimerization, such as the functionalized surface of beads (McIntosh et al., 2008) or the presence of an antibody (Powers et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous studies.

claim: NDC80 binds the 4-subunit MIS12 complex.
source: First, NDC80 binds the 4-subunit MIS12 complex, whose kinetochore recruitment, in turn, depends on the chromatin proximal kinetochore subunits CENP-C and CENP-T (Huis In 't Veld et al., 2016; Petrovic et al., 2016; Przewloka et al., 2011; Screpanti et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous studies.

claim: MIS12 complex kinetochore recruitment depends on CENP-C and CENP-T.
source: First, NDC80 binds the 4-subunit MIS12 complex, whose kinetochore recruitment, in turn, depends on the chromatin proximal kinetochore subunits CENP-C and CENP-T (Huis In 't Veld et al., 2016; Petrovic et al., 2016; Przewloka et al., 2011; Screpanti et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous studies.

claim: NDC80 is recruited by direct binding to two phosphorylated motifs near the N-terminus of CENP-T.
source: Second, NDC80 is recruited by direct binding to two phosphorylated motifs near the N-terminus of CENP-T (Huis In 't Veld et al., 2016; Gascoigne et al., 2011; Kim and Yu, 2015; Suzuki et al., 2015; Malvezzi et al., 2013; Nishino et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous studies.

claim: Kinetochores contain approximately eight NDC80 complexes per microtubule-binding site.
source: In agreement with these multiple binding modes, quantitative fluorescence microscopy and bottom-up reconstitutions indicated that kinetochores contain multiple NDC80 complexes, with recent estimates converging on eight complexes per microtubule-binding site (Huis In 't Veld et al., 2016; Suzuki et al., 2015; Weir et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous studies.

claim: A single human kinetochore contains approximately 200 NDC80 complexes that bind 15-20 microtubules.
source: In humans, a single kinetochore contains a molecular lawn of approximately 200 NDC80 complexes that bind 15–20 microtubules (Suzuki et al., 2015; Wendell et al., 1993).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous studies.

claim: Monomeric NDC80 complexes briefly interact with the microtubule lattice but do not follow the ends of depolymerizing microtubules.
source: Consistent with previous findings (Powers et al., 2009; Schmidt et al., 2012), monomeric NDC80 complexes briefly interacted with the microtubule lattice but did not follow the ends of depolymerizing microtubules (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations and supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Tip-tracking events were observed for CENP-T:NDC80 and CENP-T:MIS12:NDC80 complexes.
source: In contrast, tip-tracking events were observed for CENP-TAlexa488:NDC80 and CENP-TAlexa488:MIS12:NDC80 complexes that were purified by size-exclusion chromatography and then added to dynamic microtubules (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in the referenced figures.

claim: A stoichiometric complex of MIS12 and phosphorylated CENP-T does not bind microtubules over a 35-fold range of concentrations.
source: As predicted, this binding strictly depended on the presence of NDC80; a similarly prepared stoichiometric complex of MIS12 and phosphorylated CENP-TAlexa488 did not bind microtubules over a 35-fold range of concentrations (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Tip-tracking assemblies contained 1.5 ± 0.7 CENP-T molecules and 5 ± 2 NDC80 molecules (mean and SD, n = 27).
source: Tip-tracking assemblies contained 1.5 ± 0.7 CENP-T molecules (mean and SD), 5 ± 2 NDC80 molecules (n = 27)
evidence: This is stated in the text based on quantification of fluorescence data.

claim: Most CENP-T:MIS12:NDC80 complexes contained three NDC80 complexes per CENP-T:MIS12.
source: most complexes contained three NDC80 complexes per CENP-T:MIS12, a number that is in agreement with the biochemically determined number of NDC80 binding sites on phosphorylated CENP-T:MIS12. (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1F.

claim: The residence time of TS-NDC80 modules on taxol-stabilized microtubules increased more than ten-fold for every additional NDC80 complex.
source: The residence time of these assemblies on microtubules increased more than ten-fold for every additional NDC80 complex (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2E.

claim: Di-, tri-, and tetravalent TS-NDC80 assemblies tracked shortening microtubule tips.
source: Di-, tri-, as well as tetravalent TS-NDC80 assemblies tracked shortening microtubule tips and each additional NDC80 increased the fraction of tip-tracking assemblies (Figure 3A–C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3A-C.

claim: Each additional NDC80 complex increased the fraction of tip-tracking assemblies.
source: Di-, tri-, as well as tetravalent TS-NDC80 assemblies tracked shortening microtubule tips and each additional NDC80 increased the fraction of tip-tracking assemblies (Figure 3A–C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3A-C.

claim: Free microtubules shortened faster than microtubules with TS-NDC80 at the tip.
source: Free microtubules in the same flow chamber shortened faster than the ones with TS-NDC80 at the tip (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3D.

claim: CENP-T- and CENP-T:MIS12-mediated oligomers of NDC80 slowed down microtubule shortening.
source: CENP-T- and CENP-T:MIS12-mediated oligomers of NDC80 slowed down microtubule shortening in a similar way (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E-F.

claim: A single trivalent T1S3[NDC80]3 assembly is sufficient to couple microtubule shortening to cargo transport.
source: This suggests that a single trivalent T1S3[NDC80]3 assembly is sufficient to couple microtubule shortening to cargo transport.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the experimental data on bead tracking.

claim: Beads coated with TS-NDC80 assemblies stalled for an average of 1.5 ± 0.2 s (mean and SEM, n = 91) after initial movement with shortening microtubule tips.
source: After initial movement with the shortening microtubule tips, the beads stalled for an average of 1.5 ± 0.2 s (mean and SEM, n = 91).
evidence: This is stated in the text based on quantification of experimental data.

claim: Single trivalent T1S3[NDC80]3 stalled microtubule depolymerization at about 1.5 piconewton.
source: Single trivalent T1S3[NDC80]3 stalled microtubule depolymerization at about 1.5 piconewton (pN).
evidence: This is stated in the text based on force measurements.

claim: Stalling forces increased to maximal values of 5-6 pN with 100-1000 T1S3[NDC80]3 modules per bead.
source: Stalling forces increased to maximal values of 5–6 pN with 100–1000 T1S3[NDC80]3 modules per bead, but did not increase further with thousands of such assemblies on a single bead (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4D.

claim: Stalling forces did not increase beyond 5-6 pN with thousands of T1S3[NDC80]3 assemblies on a single bead.
source: Stalling forces increased to maximal values of 5–6 pN with 100–1000 T1S3[NDC80]3 modules per bead, but did not increase further with thousands of such assemblies on a single bead (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4D.

claim: There is a correlation between the amplitude of the stalling force and the probability of a rescue event.
source: Pooling of stall forces from beads coated with varying surface densities of T1S3[NDC80]3 and T2S2[NDC80]2 resulted in 51 detachment events (71%) and 21 rescue events (29%) and revealed a striking correlation between the amplitude of the stalling force and the probability of a rescue event (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4E.

claim: A very dense coating of monovalent T3S1[NDC80]1 on beads did not generate stalling forces higher than 3 pN.
source: Interestingly, even a very dense coating of monovalent T3S1[NDC80]1 on the beads did not generate stalling forces higher than 3 pN (Figure 4D)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4D.

claim: Monovalent T3S1[NDC80]1 never produced rescue events.
source: Interestingly, even a very dense coating of monovalent T3S1[NDC80]1 on the beads did not generate stalling forces higher than 3 pN (Figure 4D) and never produced rescue events.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on experimental observations.

claim: Multivalent NDC80 modules promote efficient coupling of microtubule-generated force.
source: Taken together, these results show that the multivalent NDC80 modules promote efficient coupling of microtubule-generated force as well as force-dependent rescue of microtubule shortening.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental results.

claim: Multivalent NDC80 modules promote force-dependent rescue of microtubule shortening.
source: Taken together, these results show that the multivalent NDC80 modules promote efficient coupling of microtubule-generated force as well as force-dependent rescue of microtubule shortening.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental results.

claim: During stalling, fluctuations along the microtubule were dampened compared to the signal across the microtubule and compared to fluctuations before and after the microtubule pulled on the bead.
source: During stalling, fluctuations along the microtubule were dampened compared to the signal across the microtubule and compared to fluctuations before and after the microtubule pulled on the bead (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 5A.

claim: Stiffening of the bead-microtubule link under force was on average two times higher during stalls produced by TS-NDC80 modules interacting with depolymerizing microtubules compared to interactions with straight protofilaments.
source: Stiffening of the bead-microtubule link under force was observed in all cases, but was on average two times higher during stalls produced by TS-NDC80 modules interacting with depolymerizing microtubules (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 5B.

claim: Force-induced stiffening of the link provided by TS-NDC80 modules is enhanced when NDC80 molecules are interacting with depolymerizing, presumably flared protofilaments, compared to straight protofilaments.
source: Apparently, force-induced stiffening of the link provided by TS-NDC80 modules is enhanced when NDC80 molecules are interacting with depolymerizing, presumably flared protofilaments, compared to when they are interacting with straight protofilaments.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: At typical picomolar concentrations of single-molecule analyses, monomeric NDC80 complexes bind weakly to microtubules and have no detectable effect on microtubule dynamics.
source: We show here that at the typical picomolar concentrations of single-molecule analyses, monomeric NDC80 complexes bind weakly to the microtubules and have no detectable effect on microtubule dynamics.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study.

claim: The integration of two NDC80 molecules in a single module is sufficient to track the tip of a shortening microtubule and to slow down microtubule depolymerization.
source: Instead, the integration of two NDC80 molecules in a single module is sufficient to track the tip of a shortening microtubule and to slow down microtubule depolymerization (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3D.

claim: Very high concentrations of monomeric NDC80 that result in complete decoration of the microtubule lattice produce a similar effect on microtubule disassembly as multivalent NDC80 modules.
source: A similar effect on microtubule disassembly had been previously observed using very high concentrations of monomeric NDC80 that resulted in complete decoration of the microtubule lattice with NDC80 (Umbreit et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to a previous study.

claim: Biased diffusion models assume that a connected ensemble of diffusive, low-affinity microtubule binding elements undergoes directional Brownian motion on a shortening microtubule.
source: Biased diffusion models assume that a connected ensemble of diffusive, low-affinity microtubule binding elements undergoes directional Brownian motion on a shortening microtubule if it can maximize its binding energy by retaining as many as possible of the binding elements bound to the microtubule lattice.
evidence: This is stated as a description of biased diffusion models.

claim: Biased diffusion models predict that net kinetochore movement is not linked to an energy expenditure by the depolymerizing microtubule.
source: By assuming that weakly bound couplers diffuse to explore the surface of the microtubule by steps that are driven by thermal energy, this model predicts that net kinetochore movement is not linked to an energy expenditure by the depolymerizing microtubule.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction of biased diffusion models.

claim: Biased diffusion models predict that attachments do not stall microtubule disassembly and have negligible effects on the speed of microtubule shortening.
source: Consequently, this type of attachment does not stall microtubule disassembly and is expected to have negligible effects on the speed of microtubule shortening (Efremov et al., 2007; Powers et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as a prediction of biased diffusion models with citations.

claim: Models in the second category predict that a fraction of the force generated by a depolymerizing microtubule is harnessed to move a non-diffusive or poorly diffusive, tightly bound coupler to the next position on the microtubule lattice.
source: Models in the second category, on the other hand, predict that a fraction of the force generated by a depolymerizing microtubule is harnessed to move a non-diffusive or poorly diffusive, tightly bound coupler to the next position on the microtubule lattice.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the second category of models.

claim: The second category of models predicts reduced microtubule disassembly rates.
source: This type of coupling is expected to result in reduced microtubule disassembly rates.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction of the second category of models.

claim: Oligomers of Dam1 (DASH) complexes bind tightly to the microtubule wall and may form microtubule-encircling rings.
source: For instance, this phenomenon has been observed in presence of oligomers of Dam1 (DASH) complexes, which bind tightly to the microtubule wall and may form microtubule-encircling rings (Westermann et al., 2005; Miranda et al., 2005; Grishchuk et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous studies.

claim: The multivalent NDC80 modules bound the microtubule tightly with residence in the range of hours.
source: The multivalent NDC80 modules generated a coupler that bound the microtubule tightly with residence in the range of hours (Figure 2)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: The multivalent NDC80 modules decreased microtubule depolymerization rates.
source: The multivalent NDC80 modules generated a coupler that bound the microtubule tightly with residence in the range of hours (Figure 2), and that decreased microtubule depolymerization rates (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: Monomeric NDC80 and monovalent T3S1[NDC80]1 did not follow or modulate microtubule shortening.
source: In contrast, and consistent with previous studies (Alushin et al., 2010; Schmidt et al., 2012), monomeric NDC80 and monovalent T3S1[NDC80]1 did not follow or modulate microtubule shortening (Figure 1B, 3BC).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations and supported by data in Figures 1B and 3BC.

claim: The stall forces produced by multivalent NDC80 modules saturated at 5-6 pN.
source: The stall forces produced by multivalent NDC80 modules saturated at 5–6 pN and increased the chance of microtubule rescue (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: The stall forces produced by multivalent NDC80 modules increased the chance of microtubule rescue.
source: The stall forces produced by multivalent NDC80 modules saturated at 5–6 pN and increased the chance of microtubule rescue (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: A significant amount of microtubule-generated energy is spent to break the bonds between the TS-NDC80 assemblies and the microtubule.
source: Comparing these values to the theoretical maximum of 13–70 pN that a microtubule can generate (Molodtsov et al., 2005; Vichare et al., 2013), we speculate that a significant amount of microtubule-generated energy is spent to break the bonds between the TS-NDC80 assemblies and the microtubule.
evidence: This is stated as speculation based on comparison with theoretical values from cited studies.

claim: Multivalent NDC80 assemblies exploit the force of depolymerizing microtubules.
source: These observations suggest a direct interaction between multivalent NDC80 assemblies and the microtubule tip, and make us suggest that these assemblies exploit the force of depolymerizing microtubules (Figure 6).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the observations.

claim: Kinetochore-oligomerized NDC80 is a friction element that slows down the speed of kinetochore movements in mitosis.
source: This conclusion is consistent with recent experiments in vivo showing that kinetochore-oligomerized NDC80 is a friction element that slows down the speed of kinetochore movements in mitosis (Long et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to a recent study.

claim: Protofilaments at growing microtubule ends are less bent than at shortening ends.
source: Protofilaments at growing microtubule ends are less bent than at shortening ends, and force-induced straightening of protofilament flares has been suggested as a mechanism to convert the energy of microtubule depolymerization into cargo transport (McIntosh et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with a citation.

claim: Force-induced straightening of protofilament flares has been suggested as a mechanism to convert the energy of microtubule depolymerization into cargo transport.
source: Protofilaments at growing microtubule ends are less bent than at shortening ends, and force-induced straightening of protofilament flares has been suggested as a mechanism to convert the energy of microtubule depolymerization into cargo transport (McIntosh et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with a citation.

claim: Externally applied opposing force slows down microtubule shortening.
source: Externally applied opposing force also slows down microtubule shortening (Franck et al., 2007), presumably through suppressed bending of depolymerizing protofilaments (Grishchuk et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated with citations.

claim: The reduced depolymerization rate of microtubules carrying TS-NDC80 assemblies supports a direct binding of multivalent NDC80 to flaring protofilaments.
source: Thus, the reduced depolymerization rate of microtubules carrying TS-NDC80 assemblies supports a direct binding of multivalent NDC80 to flaring protofilaments (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the experimental results.

claim: The correlation between the magnitude of the TS-NDC80 mediated stalling forces and the probability to reverse microtubule depolymerization into growth is a direct consequence of force-induced protofilament straightening.
source: We therefore propose that the correlation between the magnitude of the TS-NDC80 mediated stalling forces and the probability to reverse microtubule depolymerization into growth is a direct consequence of force-induced protofilament straightening.
evidence: This is stated as a proposal based on the experimental results.

claim: Kinetochore-associated fibrils that modulate the shape of depolymerizing microtubule ends at attached kinetochores have been identified in vivo using electron tomography.
source: Kinetochore-associated fibrils that modulate the shape of depolymerizing microtubule ends at attached kinetochores have previously been identified in vivo using electron tomography (McIntosh et al., 2008), but their molecular identity has remained unclear.
evidence: This is stated with a citation.

claim: The fibrils that modulate the shape of depolymerizing microtubule ends at attached kinetochores might consist of oligomers of NDC80 complexes.
source: While our studies suggest that the fibrils might consist of oligomers of NDC80 complexes, further analyses will be required for a detailed molecular dissection.
evidence: This is stated as a suggestion based on the study's findings.

claim: Stabilization of kinetochore-microtubule attachments in vivo is tension-dependent.
source: Stabilization of kinetochore-microtubule attachments in vivo is tension-dependent (Cane et al., 2013; Nicklas and Ward, 1994).
evidence: This is stated with citations.

claim: The multivalency of NDC80 at the outer kinetochore likely directly contributes to the tension-dependent stabilization of kinetochore-microtubule interactions in vivo.
source: The multivalency of NDC80 at the outer kinetochore thus likely directly contributes to the tension-dependent stabilization of kinetochore-microtubule in vivo.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the study's findings.

claim: Stabilization of kinetochore-microtubule interactions by tension has been recapitulated in vitro with purified kinetochore particles from Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
source: Stabilization of kinetochore-microtubule interactions by tension has also been recapitulated in vitro with purified kinetochore particles from Saccharomyce cerevisiae (Akiyoshi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated with a citation.

claim: Purified kinetochore particles from Saccharomyces cerevisiae lose their connection to the microtubule ends under an externally applied force of several pN.
source: These purified kinetochore particles, whose homogeneity and stoichiometry of microtubule binders has not been precisely defined, lose their connection to the microtubule ends under an externally applied force of several pN (Akiyoshi et al., 2010; Miller et al., 2016; Sarangapani et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations.

claim: The force-coupling observed for purified kinetochore particles from Saccharomyces cerevisiae appears to be crucially dependent on the Dam1 complex.
source: The force-coupling observed for the purified kinetochore particles appears to be crucially dependent on the Dam1 complex (Akiyoshi et al., 2010), an additional microtubule binder that contributes to the efficient force coupling at the microtubule plus-end in Saccharomyce cerevisiae.
evidence: This is stated with a citation.

claim: Dam1 and the functionally analogous human Ska complex confer plus-end tracking activity in vitro to monomeric NDC80.
source: Dam1, as well as the functionally analogous human Ska complex, also confer plus-end tracking activity in vitro to monomeric NDC80 (Janczyk et al., 2017; Lampert et al., 2010; Schmidt et al., 2012; Tien et al., 2010; Welburn et al., 2009; Helgeson et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citations.

claim: The organization of NDC80 in multivalent modules is at least partially sufficient to recapitulate tension-dependent stabilization of cargo-microtubule coupling in vitro.
source: In conclusion, our work highlights that recapitulating stoichiometry and spatial arrangement of macromolecular assemblies is crucial for the bottom-up reconstitution and biophysical analysis of the kinetochore. The organization of NDC80 in multivalent modules is -at least partially- sufficient to recapitulate tension-dependent stabilization of cargo-microtubule coupling in vitro.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the study.

claim: Recapitulating stoichiometry and spatial arrangement of macromolecular assemblies is crucial for the bottom-up reconstitution and biophysical analysis of the kinetochore.
source: In conclusion, our work highlights that recapitulating stoichiometry and spatial arrangement of macromolecular assemblies is crucial for the bottom-up reconstitution and biophysical analysis of the kinetochore.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the study.

claim: Phosphorylated CENP-T can recruit NDC80 complexes to p-Thr11 and p-Thr85 and a MIS12:NDC80 complex to p-Ser201.
source: We have previously shown that CENP-T that is phosphorylated by CDK1:Cyclin-B can recruit NDC80 complexes to p-Thr11 and p-Thr85 and a MIS12:NDC80 complex to p-Ser201 (Huis In 't Veld et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to previous work.

claim: A stoichiometric complex of MIS12 and phosphorylated CENP-T did not bind microtubules in a concentration range from 0.2 to 7 nM.
source: TM does not bind to microtubules and does not follow microtubule shortening in a concentration range from 0.2 to 7 nM.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The residence time of CENP-T:NDC80 assemblies on taxol-stabilized microtubules ranged from multiple seconds to multiple minutes.
source: The residence time of CENP-T:NDC80 assemblies (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) under similar conditions ranged from multiple seconds to multiple minutes (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The residence time of CENP-T:NDC80 assemblies is comparable with divalent and trivalent NDC80 TS-modules.
source: This is comparable with divalent and trivalent NDC80 TS-modules and supports the idea that NDC80 that is bound to TS modules and NDC80 that is bound to CENP-T interact with microtubules in a similar manner.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the comparison of residence times.

claim: Using the reciprocal of the residence time of T3S1[NDC80]1 as koff, stochastic simulations determined kon to be 2.6 s−1.
source: Using the reciprocal of the residence time of T3S1[NDC80]1 as koff, stochastic simulations of the residence times of mono-, di-, tri-, and tetravalent assemblies were used to determine kon (Figure 2E). A fit to the data resulted in a kon of 2.6 s−1.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on simulation results shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Assuming a TS-NDC80 assembly as a sphere, one NDC80 inside the sphere has a local concentration of 1.7 µM.
source: Assuming a TS-NDC80 assembly as a sphere, one NDC80 inside the sphere has a local concentration of 1.7 µM.
evidence: This is stated as a calculation based on the geometry of the assembly.

claim: The predicted concentration-dependent association rate is 1.5 µM−1s−1, which falls within the published range of kon for free NDC80 binding to microtubules.
source: This predicts a concentration-dependent association rate of 1.5 µM−1s−1, a value that falls well within the published range of kon for free NDC80 binding to microtubules (Powers et al., 2009; Tien et al., 2010; Zaytsev et al., 2015).
